subtype: Using skills for a purpose beyond self [Actor]
passage:
Gudi Padwa morning, gudis on bamboo poles at every window, and Eshaan was at the municipal school in Kothrud with three old laptops for twenty kids. The fourth had died on the way.
At his office job he was good, well paid, often praised. And lately, a little bored. These Saturday coding classes were where the restlessness went.
"Three laptops, twenty of us?" Deepak, thirteen, raised an eyebrow.
"Then we code on paper first," Eshaan said, and drew a robot on the board. The kids wrote instructions, move, turn, pick up, and Eshaan walked their steps like the robot, bumping into desks whenever they got the order wrong. The room roared.
By noon Deepak had a working loop on a laptop. Eshaan felt that quiet glow again. Not finished, he thought. Just getting started.

qa.q: How many laptops did Eshaan have for the twenty kids?
qa.a: Three old laptops; the fourth had died on the way.

qa.q: How does Eshaan feel about the office job, and about the class?
qa.a: Eshaan feels content but a little bored at the office, and a quiet glow in the class, where the restlessness finds a purpose.

qa.q: How did Eshaan handle the missing laptops, and what does it show?
qa.a: He switched to coding on paper and acted as the robot himself, showing that a skill can still be taught well when resources fall short.

qa.q: What is the class like for Deepak?
qa.a: Deepak starts out doubtful, raising an eyebrow at three laptops for twenty, and ends with a working loop by noon.

grounding: A young professional, content yet restless at work, puts his skills into teaching children and sees growth as ongoing.

passage:
Beatriz's shift at the bakery in Sao Paulo started at five, and the bus ride took forty minutes each way. For two years she had told herself she would start drawing properly once she could afford the illustration course, once she had a desk, once things calmed down.
Then Wei, who baked the rolls beside her, showed her a notebook full of tiny ink sketches of customers. "Bus sketches," he shrugged. "Twenty minutes a day."
So Beatriz began. A pencil, an exercise book from the corner shop, the faces on the early bus. On Sundays she borrowed drawing books from the public library. The hands were terrible at first.
Three months later Wei flipped through her book and stopped at an old man asleep against a window. "That," he said. "That's him."

qa.q: How long did the bus ride take each way?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How might Beatriz have felt when Wei stopped at the sleeping old man?
qa.a: She likely felt proud and encouraged, since after three months of terrible hands her drawing had finally caught someone.

qa.q: What did Beatriz do instead of waiting for perfect conditions?
qa.a: She started small with a pencil, a cheap exercise book, faces on the bus and library books, rather than waiting for the course, the desk or calmer times.

qa.q: How might Wei see Beatriz's progress?
qa.a: Wei, who sketches on the bus himself, probably sees it with warmth and respect, knowing how hard it is to keep going with so little time.

grounding: An adult stops waiting for money and a desk and starts sketching on the bus with a pencil and library books.

passage:
On Halloween evening in their Toronto apartment, Ivan was already in his green dinosaur costume, tail dragging, but his sneakers were still untied. Rania knelt to help.
"No! Me do it!" He pushed her hand away.
Rania sat back on her heels. Outside, kids were already shrieking down the hall. Ivan made one loop, then another, lost both, and started again, tongue poking out. On the fourth try the bow held, lopsided.
He jumped up and stamped. "Look, Mama! I did it MYSELF!"
"You did," Rania said, and let him lead the way to the door.

qa.q: On which try did the bow hold?
qa.a: On the fourth try.

qa.q: How does Ivan feel when the bow finally holds?
qa.a: He feels proud and delighted, jumping, stamping and shouting that he did it himself.

qa.q: What did Rania do that supported Ivan's independence?
qa.a: She sat back and waited, even with other kids already out in the hall, letting him try four times instead of taking over.

qa.q: What might waiting have been like for Rania?
qa.a: Rania probably felt a little impatient with the shrieking already in the hall, but chose patience so Ivan could finish on his own.

grounding: A young child pushes his mother's hand away and ties his own laces, proud of doing it himself.

subtype: Wants to choose own subject and friends [Actor]
passage:
The Rath Yatra crowds were thick outside when Sachin spread the Class 11 form on the dining table. It had to be submitted by ten tomorrow.
He ticked Humanities.
His mother, Rukmini, saw it from the kitchen door. "Science. We agreed. And no more of that theatre group. They're the reason your marks slipped."
"You agreed," Sachin said. His voice shook, but he kept going. "I love history. And those are my friends, Maa. I chose them."
"At your age you don't know what's good for you."
"Then when do I start knowing?"
The drums of the procession rolled past the window. Neither of them moved. Sachin kept his hand flat on the form, as if someone might take it.

qa.q: By what time did the form have to be submitted?
qa.a: By ten tomorrow.

qa.q: What does Sachin keeping a hand flat on the form suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He feels nervous but determined, afraid the choice will be taken from him, because choosing his stream and friends feels like part of who he is.

qa.q: What could Sachin try so the talk becomes less of a clash?
qa.a: Explain calmly why history matters to him and what the theatre friends give him, and ask to talk it through with a teacher or counsellor before ten tomorrow.

qa.q: Why might Rukmini react so strongly?
qa.a: Rukmini likely feels worried about his future, blames the theatre group for the slipping marks, and sees science as the safe route.

grounding: A teenager ticks the stream he wants and defends the friends he chose, clashing with his mother's plans.

subtype: Forging own path despite family pressure [Actor]
passage:
Manali, Lohri night
Dear Harsha,
They lit a small Lohri fire outside the institute tonight, in the snow, and I thought of Biji's rewri and our terrace back in Amritsar. I miss them so much it aches.
Papa still isn't speaking to me properly. He tells relatives I'm "taking a break" from engineering. Mama sends parathas by courier with a message: "Come back when you're done with this madness."
But Harsha, yesterday I led six trainees across a frozen stream, and I have never felt so awake. I know there's no fixed salary, no clear ladder, and I might fail. I'd rather fail at this than succeed at something that makes me feel asleep.
I call them every Sunday, even when it's short. I love them. I'm just not going back to engineering.
Gurleen

qa.q: How many trainees did Gurleen lead across a frozen stream?
qa.a: Six trainees.

qa.q: How does Gurleen feel about the new path and about the family?
qa.a: Gurleen feels wide awake and alive in the mountains, while aching with homesickness and love for a family that disapproves.

qa.q: What could help Gurleen keep both the path and the family?
qa.a: Keep up the Sunday calls, share small real moments from training, and perhaps invite Papa to see the work, while accepting that approval may take time.

qa.q: How might Papa see Gurleen's choice?
qa.a: Papa seems hurt and embarrassed, calling it a break in front of relatives, probably worried about the risk and the lost engineering route.

grounding: A young adult trains for an unusual mountain career despite family disapproval, while still loving and calling them.

passage:
Dear Shalini Didi,
I know Mummy told you I said no to the Ludhiana plan. I want you to hear my reasons from me, not from the family group.
I'm not refusing the shop because I don't care. I'm staying in Bengaluru because I've just been given the lead on the school-bus routing project, and I want to see if I can do it. Leaving midway would let my team down too.
But I'm not walking away. I'll come home every second month, and I have already booked leave for Papa's knee operation in March. Tell me honestly if that isn't enough, and we'll work something out together. You know the shop far better than I do. I'm listening.
Your brother,
Baljeet

qa.q: What project has Baljeet just been given the lead on?
qa.a: The school-bus routing project.

qa.q: Why does Baljeet want Shalini to hear the reasons directly?
qa.a: Baljeet feels anxious that the family will think Baljeet doesn't care, and wants to be understood rather than seen as defiant.

qa.q: What makes Baljeet's letter a balanced response rather than simple defiance?
qa.a: Baljeet explains the reasons, names the duties that will be kept, like visits every second month and leave for Papa's operation, and invites Shalini's honest view.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Shalini may still be disappointed about the shop, but likely feels respected and reassured by Baljeet's honesty and concrete promises.

grounding: An adult keeps a chosen career while honouring family and team duties, explaining the reasons and staying open.

subtype: Wants warm, sweet, soft things now [Actor]
passage:
Daycare note, Thursday
Thomas had a sunny morning. He loved the bubble machine and cried hard when it was switched off. A cuddle and his soft blanket settled him. At snack he asked for "more sweet" after his banana and was cross for a minute when we said all gone.
At pick-up his big sister Trisha laughed: "He cries every time the fun stops!" Tomorrow we will warn him before the bubbles end.

qa.q: What did Thomas ask for after his banana?
qa.a: "More sweet."

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when the bubble machine was switched off?
qa.a: He felt upset and cried hard, because the happy, bubbly fun stopped all at once.

qa.q: What will the caregiver try tomorrow, and why?
qa.a: Warning Thomas before the bubbles end, so the stop feels less sudden and easier for him to handle.

qa.q: How does Trisha see her brother's crying?
qa.a: Trisha finds it funny, laughing that he cries every time the fun stops.

grounding: A toddler delights in bubbles, cuddles and sweet things and cries when they stop, as his sister notices.

subtype: Pleasure versus duty in the hostel [Actor]
passage: Minakshi, you think your Hafsa Khala was always the serious one? Let me tell you about the first monsoon night at my hostel in Mumbai. I was nineteen, the anatomy test was next morning, and our study group was meeting at nine. Then the rain came down like a curtain, and my roommates dragged me out to Marine Drive. We ate roasted bhutta with lime and chilli, soaked to the bone, waves crashing over the wall, laughing till our stomachs hurt. I can still taste that corn. But every few minutes a small voice said: the study group, the test. I got back at one, dripping, and read two chapters by torchlight. I wouldn't give that night back. I also never skipped a group again without telling them.

qa.q: What did Hafsa and the roommates eat at Marine Drive?
qa.a: Roasted bhutta with lime and chilli.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling during the night out?
qa.a: Hafsa felt pure joy, laughing in the rain, with a pinch of guilt from the small voice reminding her of the study group and the test.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside the story, and what did Hafsa take from it?
qa.a: Coming back at one and reading two chapters by torchlight; Hafsa kept the joy but decided never again to skip the group without telling them.

qa.q: How might the study group have felt when Hafsa didn't show up?
qa.a: They may have felt let down or confused, waiting without a word from Hafsa.

grounding: An elder recalls skipping a study group for a rainy night out, enjoying it fully with a pinch of guilt.

subtype: Savouring without being ruled by it [Response]
passage:
A year ago I was the guy who ate lunch over the keyboard and spent weekends chasing the next big thing: a trek booked on a whim, a new gadget, a night out that ended at 4 a.m. and left me wrecked till Tuesday. None of it ever felt like enough.
Divyansh changed that without meaning to. One Sunday he made rajma-chawal from scratch and made me sit on his balcony and actually eat it, slowly, no phone. "Tarun, taste it," he kept saying.
Now I take a full lunch break away from the desk. Saturday mornings are for football with the colony kids, Sunday afternoons for a nap, no guilt. I still go out, but I'm home by midnight, because Monday matters too. Pleasure was never the problem. Rushing through it was.

qa.q: What did Divyansh make from scratch one Sunday?
qa.a: Rajma-chawal.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel about the constant chasing a year ago?
qa.a: Tarun felt restless and never satisfied; the treks, gadgets and late nights never felt like enough and left him wrecked till Tuesday.

qa.q: Which of Tarun's new habits would you suggest to someone always chasing the next thrill?
qa.a: Taking a full lunch break away from the desk, keeping regular play and rest, and coming home by midnight so pleasure fits alongside work.

qa.q: Why might Divyansh have insisted that Tarun eat slowly on the balcony?
qa.a: Divyansh probably cared about his friend and wanted him to actually enjoy the meal instead of rushing through it like everything else.

grounding: An adult learns to savour meals, rest and play and keeps pleasure in balance instead of chasing the next thrill.
